title: Types of Chemical Reactions
description: Patterns of reactivity: classifying reactions, reactions in water, redox and the activity series.
overview: There are millions of chemical reactions, but a short list of patterns covers most of them. Recognizing the pattern lets a chemist predict the products of a reaction never seen before, which is the practical skill of inorganic and general chemistry.

This chapter starts with the five classic types, then looks at reactions in water, where ions in solution give three recurring outcomes: a precipitate forms, an acid neutralizes a base, or electrons are transferred. It ends with the half-reaction method for balancing redox equations and the activity series.
objectives: Classify a reaction as synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement or combustion.
Use solubility rules to predict precipitates, and write molecular, complete ionic and net ionic equations.
Recognize acid–base neutralization and gas-forming reactions.
Assign oxidation states, identify what is oxidized and reduced, and name the oxidizing and reducing agents.
Balance redox equations by the half-reaction method in acid and in base.
Use the activity series to predict displacement reactions.

subs.title: Synthesis reactions
body: Two or more simple substances combine into one more complex product. Look for several reactants and one product. These reactions usually release energy.

subs.title: Decomposition reactions
body: One compound breaks into two or more simpler substances. It is the reverse of synthesis and usually needs heat, light or electricity.

eqs: catalyzed by MnO₂ or an enzyme

subs.title: Single replacement
body: One element takes the place of another in a compound. A metal replaces another metal, or hydrogen, only if it is more reactive. A halogen replaces a less reactive halogen. The activity series, below, predicts which reactions go.

eqs: a metal displaces hydrogen from an acid

subs.title: Double replacement
body: Two compounds swap partners. These reactions typically occur between ionic compounds in water and are driven by one product leaving the solution: an insoluble solid, a gas, or a weak electrolyte such as water. No electrons are transferred.

subs.title: Combustion
body: A substance reacts rapidly with oxygen, releasing heat and often light. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon or an alcohol gives CO₂ and H₂O. With limited oxygen, incomplete combustion also produces carbon monoxide and soot.

body.note: These categories overlap. Combustion of a metal, like 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, is also a synthesis, and single replacement is also a redox reaction. Classes are guides to prediction, not exclusive boxes.

check.q: Fe + CuCl₂ → FeCl₂ + Cu is a…
Heating CaCO₃ gives CaO and CO₂. This is a…

sections.title: Reactions in aqueous solution
body: Water dissolves many ionic compounds by separating them into ions. A solute that produces ions and conducts electricity is an **electrolyte**. A **strong electrolyte** is fully dissociated: soluble ionic compounds, strong acids and strong bases. A **weak electrolyte** (acetic acid, ammonia) is only partly ionized. A **nonelectrolyte** (sugar, ethanol) stays as molecules.
A **precipitate** is an insoluble solid that forms when ions combine in solution. Whether a compound is soluble follows empirical **solubility rules**:

head: Compounds containing…
Soluble?
Exceptions
rows: Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Pb²⁺; Ca²⁺ and Ag⁺ slightly
Group 1 and NH₄⁺ (sulfides also of Group 2)
table.caption: Solubility rules for ionic compounds in water.

body: Three kinds of equation describe the same reaction. For silver nitrate and sodium chloride:

eq: Complete ionic:  Ag⁺ + NO₃⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) + Na⁺ + NO₃⁻

body: **Spectator ions** (Na⁺, NO₃⁻) appear unchanged on both sides and are removed to give the **net ionic equation**, which shows only what actually reacts. Write soluble strong electrolytes as ions. Write solids, liquids, gases and weak electrolytes in molecular form.

example.title: Predicting a precipitate
example.problem: Will a precipitate form when solutions of Na₂CO₃ and CaCl₂ are mixed? Write the net ionic equation.
solution: Swapping partners gives CaCO₃ and NaCl. By the rules, carbonates are insoluble (Ca²⁺ is not an exception) and chlorides are soluble. CaCO₃ precipitates.

body.tip: Solubility is quantified by the solubility product, Ksp. See the chapter on aqueous equilibria.

What are the spectator ions when KOH and HNO₃ react?

sections.title: Acid–base and gas-forming reactions
body: In a **neutralization** an acid reacts with a base to give a salt and water. The common strong acids are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first proton), HClO₄ and HClO₃. The common strong bases are the hydroxides of Group 1 and of Ca, Sr and Ba. Strong acids and bases are fully dissociated, so for any of them the net ionic equation is the same:
A weak acid or base appears in molecular form: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. A neutralization releases about 56 kJ per mole of water formed for strong acid with strong base.

Some double replacements remove a product as a gas. Carbonates and bicarbonates react with acids to give CO₂, sulfites give SO₂, and sulfides give H₂S. The intermediate acids H₂CO₃ and H₂SO₃ decompose:
The definitions of acids and bases, and the quantitative treatment of pH, are in the chapter on acids and bases.

What gas is released when limestone reacts with vinegar?

sections.title: Oxidation–reduction reactions
body: In a **redox** reaction, electrons are transferred. **Oxidation** is the loss of electrons and **reduction** is the gain of electrons (“OIL RIG”: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain). The two always occur together. The species oxidized is the **reducing agent**, since it supplies the electrons. The species reduced is the **oxidizing agent**.
To follow electrons in covalent compounds, chemists assign **oxidation states**, the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic, with shared electrons given to the more electronegative atom.

list: An atom in an element has oxidation state 0 (Na, O₂, S₈).
A monatomic ion has an oxidation state equal to its charge.
The oxidation states in a species add up to its total charge.
Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2 in compounds. F is −1.
H is +1 (−1 in metal hydrides such as NaH). O is −2 (−1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂).
Other halogens are −1, except in compounds with O or F.

body: A rise in oxidation state is oxidation, and a drop is reduction.

example.title: Assigning oxidation states
example.problem: Find the oxidation state of (a) Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻, (b) N in NO₃⁻ and in NH₄⁺, (c) Mn in MnO₄⁻.
solution: (a) 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so x = +6. (b) x + 3(−2) = −1 gives +5 for N in NO₃⁻; x + 4(+1) = +1 gives −3 for N in NH₄⁺. (c) x + 4(−2) = −1, so Mn is +7.

example.title: Identifying the agents
example.problem: In 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, what is oxidized and what is reduced?
example.solution: Al goes from 0 to +3: oxidized, so Al is the reducing agent. Fe goes from +3 to 0: reduced, so Fe₂O₃ is the oxidizing agent. This is the thermite reaction.

body: In **disproportionation** a single species is both oxidized and reduced. For example, chlorine in cold dilute base: Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O (Cl goes from 0 to −1 and to +1).

check.q: In MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺, the oxidizing agent is…
check.why: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so it is reduced; its species is the oxidizing agent.

check.q: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in H₂SO₄?

sections.title: Balancing redox equations
body: Redox equations must balance atoms and charge, so electrons lost must equal electrons gained. The **half-reaction method** splits the reaction into an oxidation and a reduction, balances each, then combines them.

list: Write and balance each half-reaction for all elements except O and H.
Balance O by adding H₂O. Balance H by adding H⁺.
Multiply the half-reactions so that the electrons cancel, and add them.
In basic solution, add OH⁻ to both sides equal to the number of H⁺, combine H⁺ and OH⁻ into H₂O, and cancel duplicate water.

example.title: In acid: permanganate and iron(II)
example.problem: Balance MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ in acidic solution.

example.title: In base: permanganate and iodide
example.problem: Balance MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ → MnO₂ + I₂ in basic solution.
solution: Each half-reaction was balanced in acid first (MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 2H₂O), then 4OH⁻ was added to both sides to neutralize the H⁺.

check.q: In the half-reaction MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ in acid, how many electrons are on the left?
In the half-reaction method for a basic solution, you first balance as if in acid, then…
check.a: Add OH⁻ to both sides to turn H⁺ into water

sections.title: The activity series
body: The **activity series** ranks metals by how easily they are oxidized. A metal displaces any ion below it in the series from solution, and a metal above hydrogen displaces H₂ from acid.

body.eq: Li > K > Ba > Ca > Na > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Ni > Sn > Pb > (H) > Cu > Ag > Au

list: Li, K, Ba, Ca and Na react with cold water to give H₂ and the hydroxide.
Mg reacts with steam; Al, Zn and Fe react with acids but not with cold water.
Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with ordinary acids. Cu dissolves in oxidizing HNO₃, which reacts through nitrate, not H⁺.
For the halogens the order is F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, so Cl₂ oxidizes Br⁻ but not F⁻.

body: The series follows from standard reduction potentials, as explained in the chapter on electrochemistry. It also explains galvanized steel: zinc is above iron, so it is oxidized first and protects the steel beneath.

example.title: Predicting a displacement
example.problem: Will a reaction occur? (a) Cu + ZnSO₄, (b) Zn + CuSO₄, (c) Br₂ + NaCl.
example.solution: (a) No: Cu is below Zn. (b) Yes: Zn is above Cu, giving ZnSO₄ + Cu. (c) No: Br₂ is less reactive than Cl₂.

check.q: Which metal will react with dilute HCl to give hydrogen?
Why does a zinc coating protect steel?
check.a: Zinc is more easily oxidized than iron, so it corrodes first
wrong: Zinc is less reactive than iron
Zinc reacts with water to form a seal

summary: Five classic types: synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement and combustion. The classes overlap, and they are guides to predict products.
In water, strong electrolytes dissociate. Solubility rules predict precipitates. A net ionic equation drops spectator ions.
Neutralization is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O for strong acids and bases. Carbonates and sulfides react with acids to give gases.
Oxidation is loss of electrons, with a rise in oxidation state. The reducing agent is oxidized and the oxidizing agent is reduced.
The half-reaction method balances atoms and charge. In base, convert H⁺ to water with OH⁻.
More active metals displace less active ones from solution.

problems.q: Write the molecular, complete ionic and net ionic equations for the reaction of aqueous Pb(NO₃)₂ with aqueous Na₂SO₄.
problems.solution: Molecular: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq). Complete ionic: Pb²⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ + 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄(s) + 2Na⁺ + 2NO₃⁻. Spectators Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ cancel.

problems.q: Balance in acidic solution: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + C₂H₅OH → Cr³⁺ + CH₃COOH.
problems.solution: Reduction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Oxidation: C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Multiply reduction by 2 and oxidation by 3 (12 electrons) and add: 2Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 28H⁺ + 3C₂H₅OH + 3H₂O → 4Cr³⁺ + 14H₂O + 3CH₃COOH + 12H⁺. Cancel: 2Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 16H⁺ + 3C₂H₅OH → 4Cr³⁺ + 11H₂O + 3CH₃COOH.

problems.q: Find the oxidation state of each element: (a) S in S₂O₃²⁻, (b) C in CH₃OH, (c) Cl in HClO₃, (d) Fe in Fe₃O₄.
Predict the products, or write no reaction: (a) Mg + Zn(NO₃)₂, (b) Ag + HCl, (c) I₂ + NaBr.
problems.solution: (a) Mg is above Zn: Mg(NO₃)₂ + Zn. (b) Ag is below H: no reaction. (c) I₂ is less reactive than Br₂: no reaction.
